title: The processing system and the programmable logic

steps.title: One chip, two halves
steps.body: Left: the hard processing system, always present and the part everything in this repository uses. Right: the FPGA fabric, empty at power-on. Below: the AXI bus pair between them. The other boards of this repository have nothing like the right-hand half.

steps.title: Two ordinary 32-bit CPU cores
steps.body: Cortex-A9, ARMv7 with NEON, up to 667 MHz on this speed grade. Linux sees two CPUs and an SMP kernel works as on any ARM board; the second core is released by kernel code through the SCU, not by PSCI firmware.

steps.title: On-chip RAM is where it all starts
steps.body: The BootROM copies `BOOT.BIN` into the 256 KiB on-chip memory (OCM) because the DDR does not exist yet. The SPL runs from there until `ps7_init` has made DDR usable.

steps.title: The DDR controller is configured by software
steps.body: On other SoCs a boot ROM or a vendor firmware blob trains the memory. Here the SPL replays register values generated for this board's DDR3L chips; get them wrong and the board never reaches U-Boot.

steps.title: Peripherals live on MIO pins
steps.body: UART0, the SD host, Ethernet, USB, QSPI and I2C are hard blocks routed to 54 multiplexed pins. They work without a bitstream. This is why the first boot is PS-only.

steps.anchor: PL  ·  PROGRAMMABLE LOGIC  (an FPGA, empty at power-on)
steps.title: The fabric is a blank slate
steps.body: Artix-7 class logic: 53,200 LUTs, 106,400 flip-flops, 140 block RAMs and 220 DSP slices on the XC7Z020. It does nothing until a configuration (a bitstream) is loaded, and it forgets it at every power cycle.

steps.title: The Zmod connectors belong to the fabric
steps.body: The SYZYGY ports have their own I/O banks wired to the PL, not to the processors. A Zmod ADC is therefore invisible to Linux until a PL design and a driver exist (chapter 13).

steps.anchor: AXI interconnect between PS and PL
steps.title: The bus pair that joins them
steps.body: General-purpose ports let the CPUs read and write registers in the fabric; high-performance ports let fabric masters, such as a DMA engine, write straight into DDR; interrupts and clocks go the same way. A design's address map comes from Vivado.

steps.anchor: HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE OTHER BOARDS OF THIS REPOSITORY
steps.title: What changes for you
steps.body: No secure monitor and no 64-bit exception levels to study, but a first stage that depends on this board's hardware design, and a second half of the chip that you program. Everything that follows in chapters 01 to 12 is the PS; chapter 13 starts on the PL.
